title: Protocol - Anaphylaxis After Vaccination
text:
========================================================================
HOPEWELL COMMUNITY CLINIC
15 Moringa Street, Khomasdal, Windhoek, Namibia
Tel: +264 61 555 0100 | Emergency line: +264 61 555 0199 (fictional)
FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION RECORD - NOT REAL PATIENT DATA
========================================================================
PROTOCOL - ANAPHYLAXIS AFTER VACCINATION
Document ID: HCC-CLN-001
Date: 2026-03-01
========================================================================
For trained clinical staff. Based on standard anaphylaxis guidance.
Approved by DOC-001 Dr Anna-Marie van Wyk, 2026-03-01. Review date: 2027-03-01.

RECOGNISE
Sudden onset (usually within 30 minutes) of breathing difficulty, wheeze, swelling of
the lips or throat, widespread rash, collapse or low blood pressure.
Do not confuse with fainting: a faint has a slow pulse, pale skin and quick recovery
when lying flat, with no rash or wheeze.

TREAT
1. Call for help. Lay the patient flat with legs raised (sitting up if breathing is
   difficult; recovery position if unconscious).
2. Give adrenaline 1 mg/mL INTRAMUSCULARLY into the outer thigh:
   0.01 mL/kg (0.01 mg/kg), maximum 0.5 mL (0.5 mg) adult, 0.3 mL child 6-12 years,
   0.15 mL child under 6 years.
3. Repeat after 5 minutes if there is no improvement.
4. Give oxygen if available (15 L/min by mask). Monitor breathing and pulse.
5. Start IV fluids (normal saline 20 mL/kg) if blood pressure is low and a line can
   be placed.
6. Transfer every patient with anaphylaxis to hospital, even after recovery, because
   symptoms can return within 12 hours.

AFTER THE EVENT
- Record the vaccine, batch number, time and treatment in the patient file.
- Report the reaction on the national adverse-event (AEFI) form within 24 hours.
- Write the allergy on the patient's clinic card.

ANAPHYLAXIS KIT CHECKLIST (checked weekly, last check 2026-11-16 by NUR-002)
- Adrenaline 1 mg/mL ampoules x 3 (expiry 2027-05-31)
- 1 mL syringes and 25 mm needles x 5
- Oxygen cylinder and mask (cylinder full)
- IV cannulas, giving set, normal saline 1 L x 2
- Blood pressure machine and pulse oximeter

Every vaccination session must have an anaphylaxis kit (adrenaline, syringes) ready.
Observe every vaccinated person for 15 minutes.
Clinic record: no anaphylaxis after vaccination in 2025 or 2026.

ABOUT THE CLINIC
Hopewell Community Clinic is a primary health care clinic serving Khomasdal,
Okahandja Park and Havana. About 1 900 patients are registered. The clinic has one
doctor (two days a week), two nurses and a clinic clerk.

OPENING HOURS
- Monday to Friday: 07:30 - 17:00 (last patient registered at 16:00)
- Saturday: 08:00 - 12:00 (immunisation and minor ailments only)
- Sunday and public holidays: closed
- Holiday closure: 24 December 2026 to 2 January 2027
For emergencies when the clinic is closed, call the emergency line
+264 61 555 0199 (fictional) or go to Katutura State Hospital or Windhoek Central
Hospital casualty, which are open 24 hours.

SERVICES BY DAY
DAY         SERVICE                                         WHO
Monday      Immunisation, child health, family planning     Nurses
Tuesday     Doctor consultations, chronic care review       Doctor + nurses
Wednesday   Antenatal care (morning), HIV testing           Nurses
Thursday    Doctor consultations, minor procedures          Doctor + nurses
Friday      Chronic medicine collection, wound care         Nurses
Saturday    Immunisation, minor ailments                    Nurse on duty

Basic laboratory tests done at the clinic: blood glucose, HbA1c, haemoglobin,
urine dipstick, pregnancy test, rapid HIV and malaria tests. Other samples are sent
to the Namibia Institute of Pathology; results take 3-5 working days.

FEES
- Consultation: N$ 10 (free for children under 5, pregnant women and pensioners)
- Chronic medicine collection: free
- Immunisation: free

WHAT TO BRING
- Your clinic card or ID document
- The child's Road-to-Health booklet for immunisation visits
- All medicines you currently take, in their boxes
- Any letters or results from other hospitals

CHRONIC MEDICINE COLLECTION
Patients with stable high blood pressure or diabetes may collect medicine every
month on Fridays without seeing the doctor. A review with the doctor is needed every
6 months, or sooner if readings are not controlled.

COMPLAINTS AND COMPLIMENTS
Speak to the clinic clerk or write in the book at reception. The clinic manager
replies within 10 working days.

CHILDHOOD IMMUNISATION SCHEDULE
Document ID: HCC-PUB-002
Date: 2026-01-15
========================================================================
This is the routine childhood schedule followed at the clinic. It follows the national
Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI). Always bring the Road-to-Health booklet.

AGE              VACCINES GIVEN                                          HOW
At birth         BCG (tuberculosis)                                      Injection, right upper arm
                 OPV 0 (oral polio)                                      2 drops by mouth
6 weeks          Pentavalent 1 (diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough,     Injection, left thigh
                 hepatitis B, Hib)
                 OPV 1                                                   2 drops by mouth
                 PCV 1 (pneumococcal)                                    Injection, right thigh
                 Rotavirus 1                                             Drops by mouth
10 weeks         Pentavalent 2, OPV 2, PCV 2, Rotavirus 2                As above
14 weeks         Pentavalent 3, OPV 3, PCV 3, IPV (injectable polio)     As above
9 months         Measles-Rubella 1 (MR1)                                 Injection, right upper arm
18 months        Measles-Rubella 2 (MR2), DTP booster                    Injections
Girls 9-14 years HPV (cervical cancer prevention), 1 dose                Injection, upper arm

VITAMIN A AND DEWORMING
- Vitamin A at 6 months, 12 months and then every 6 months until 5 years
- Deworming (albendazole) every 6 months from 12 months

AFTER VACCINATION - WHAT IS NORMAL
- Mild fever, crying or a sore, red spot where the injection was given for 1-2 days
- A small sore that forms a scar at the BCG site after 2-6 weeks (this is expected)
Give paracetamol syrup by weight if the child has fever, and keep breastfeeding.

COME BACK TO THE CLINIC IF
- Fever lasts more than 2 days, or the child has a fit (convulsion)
- The child is very sleepy, will not feed, or has difficulty breathing
- Swelling of the face or lips, or a widespread rash (allergic reaction)

MISSED A DOSE?
Come to any immunisation day. Missed doses are caught up; the schedule does not
restart. Children up to 5 years can catch up on missed vaccines.

title: Emergency Guide - Choking
text:
========================================================================
HOPEWELL COMMUNITY CLINIC
15 Moringa Street, Khomasdal, Windhoek, Namibia
Tel: +264 61 555 0100 | Emergency line: +264 61 555 0199 (fictional)
FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION RECORD - NOT REAL PATIENT DATA
========================================================================
EMERGENCY GUIDE - CHOKING
Document ID: HCC-PUB-004
Date: 2026-02-01
========================================================================
Follows standard first-aid practice (Red Cross / resuscitation council guidance).

SIGNS OF SEVERE CHOKING
- Cannot speak, cry, breathe or cough
- Clutching the throat, face turning blue or grey
- Mild choking: can still cough and speak - encourage coughing, do not slap the back

ADULT OR CHILD OVER 1 YEAR WHO CANNOT BREATHE, COUGH OR SPEAK
1. If they can cough, encourage them to keep coughing.
2. If they cannot cough: stand behind them, lean them forward and give up to 5 firm
   back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
3. If still choking: give up to 5 abdominal thrusts - fist just above the belly
   button, pull sharply inwards and upwards.
4. Repeat 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. Call for help / the emergency line.
5. If they become unresponsive, start CPR and get emergency help.

PREGNANT WOMEN AND VERY LARGE ADULTS
Use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts: stand behind, place your fist on the
middle of the breastbone and pull sharply backwards.

BABY UNDER 1 YEAR
- Lay the baby face down along your forearm, head lower than the body, and give up
  to 5 back blows.
- Then turn the baby face up and give up to 5 chest thrusts with two fingers in the
  centre of the chest. Do NOT use abdominal thrusts on a baby.
- Check the mouth after each round; remove an object only if you can see it.
  Never sweep blindly with a finger.

WHEN YOU CALL FOR HELP, SAY
- "Someone is choking and cannot breathe"
- Age of the person and where you are (nearest landmark)
- What you have done so far

AFTERWARDS
Anyone who received abdominal thrusts must be checked by a health worker afterwards,
because the thrusts can cause internal injury.

PREVENTION FOR SMALL CHILDREN
Cut grapes and sausages lengthways, keep coins, batteries and small toys out of reach,
and always sit with a child who is eating.

HOPEWELL COMMUNITY CLINIC
15 Moringa Street, Khomasdal, Windhoek, Namibia
Tel: +264 61 555 0100 | Emergency line: +264 61 555 0199 (fictional)
FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION RECORD - NOT REAL PATIENT DATA
========================================================================
EMERGENCY GUIDE - SEVERE BLEEDING
Document ID: HCC-PUB-005
Date: 2026-02-01
========================================================================
Follows standard first-aid practice.

1. Protect yourself: use gloves or a plastic bag over your hand if you can.
2. Press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth or dressing.
3. Keep pressing without stopping for at least 10 minutes. If blood soaks through,
   add more cloth on top - do not remove the first one.
4. If possible, have the person lie down and raise their legs if there is no leg
   injury.
5. Call the emergency line or bring the person to the clinic or hospital.
6. Do not remove objects stuck in a wound; press around them instead.

LIFE-THREATENING BLEEDING FROM AN ARM OR LEG
If firm pressure does not stop blood spurting from an arm or leg, and you are trained,
a tourniquet may be applied 5-7 cm above the wound. Note the time it was applied and
tell the ambulance crew. Never apply a tourniquet to the neck, head or body.

NOSEBLEED
Sit up, lean forward, pinch the soft part of the nose for 10-15 minutes and breathe
through the mouth. Do not tip the head back. Get help if bleeding lasts more than
20 minutes, or after a head injury.

SIGNS OF SHOCK (URGENT HOSPITAL CARE)
- Pale, cold, sweaty skin
- Fast, weak pulse and fast breathing
- Confusion, drowsiness or fainting
Keep the person lying down and warm with a blanket, and do not give food or drink.

PATIENTS ON BLOOD THINNERS
People who take warfarin or similar medicines bleed for longer. Even small wounds
should be checked at the clinic.

text:

HOPEWELL COMMUNITY CLINIC
15 Moringa Street, Khomasdal, Windhoek, Namibia
Tel: +264 61 555 0100 | Emergency line: +264 61 555 0199 (fictional)
FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION RECORD - NOT REAL PATIENT DATA
========================================================================
EMERGENCY GUIDE - BURNS
Document ID: HCC-PUB-006
Date: 2026-02-01
========================================================================
Follows standard first-aid practice.

1. Stop the burning: move away from the heat source. If clothes are on fire: stop,
   drop and roll, or smother the flames with a blanket.
2. Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes. Cooling
   still helps up to 3 hours after the burn.
3. Remove rings, watches and clothing near the burn unless stuck to the skin.
4. Cover loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag (lengthways, not wrapped
   tightly around a limb).
5. Do NOT apply ice, butter, oil, toothpaste, egg white or traditional remedies.
6. Do not burst blisters.
7. Keep the person warm - especially small children, who lose heat quickly.

PAIN
Paracetamol or ibuprofen by the dose on the package can be given for pain.

GO TO THE CLINIC OR HOSPITAL IF
- The burn is larger than the person's palm, is deep, or on the face, hands, feet,
  genitals or over a joint
- The person is a child, elderly, pregnant or has diabetes
- The burn is from electricity or chemicals
- The person breathed in smoke (hoarse voice, coughing, soot around the nose)

CHEMICAL BURNS
Brush off dry powder first, then rinse with plenty of running water for at least
20 minutes. Keep the chemical container to show the health worker.

ELECTRICAL BURNS
Switch off the power before touching the person. Electrical burns can damage the
heart even when the skin burn looks small - always go to hospital.

PARAFFIN STOVE AND OPEN FIRE SAFETY
Most burns in children at home come from hot water, paraffin stoves and open fires.
Keep children away from cooking areas and turn pot handles inwards.

title: Emergency Guide - Stroke and Heart Attack
text:
========================================================================
HOPEWELL COMMUNITY CLINIC
15 Moringa Street, Khomasdal, Windhoek, Namibia
Tel: +264 61 555 0100 | Emergency line: +264 61 555 0199 (fictional)
FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION RECORD - NOT REAL PATIENT DATA
========================================================================
EMERGENCY GUIDE - STROKE AND HEART ATTACK
Document ID: HCC-PUB-007
Date: 2026-02-01
========================================================================
Follows standard first-aid practice.

STROKE - think FAST
- Face: has one side of the face dropped?
- Arms: can they lift both arms and keep them up?
- Speech: is their speech slurred or confused?
- Time: call for emergency help immediately. Note the time the signs started.
Other signs: sudden loss of vision, sudden severe headache, loss of balance.
Do not give food, drink or medicines to someone who may be having a stroke.
Lay them on their side if they are drowsy or vomiting.

Treatment in hospital works best within the first few hours - do not wait to see if
the signs go away.

HEART ATTACK
Signs: chest pain or pressure that may spread to the arm, neck, jaw or back;
shortness of breath; sweating; nausea. Women, older people and people with diabetes
may have only breathlessness, tiredness or upper stomach pain.
1. Call for emergency help immediately.
2. Sit the person down and keep them calm.
3. If they are not allergic and are able to chew, give one adult aspirin (300 mg)
   to chew slowly.
4. If they have their own heart spray (GTN), help them use it.
5. If they become unresponsive and are not breathing normally, start CPR.

CPR (ADULT)
Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, 100-120 times a minute, at least 5 cm
deep. If an automated defibrillator (AED) is available, switch it on and follow the
voice instructions.

PEOPLE AT HIGHER RISK
High blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, high cholesterol and being overweight raise
the risk of stroke and heart attack. Taking chronic medicine every day lowers it.

title: Emergency Guide - Snakebite
text:

HOPEWELL COMMUNITY CLINIC
15 Moringa Street, Khomasdal, Windhoek, Namibia
Tel: +264 61 555 0100 | Emergency line: +264 61 555 0199 (fictional)
FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION RECORD - NOT REAL PATIENT DATA
========================================================================
EMERGENCY GUIDE - SNAKEBITE
Document ID: HCC-PUB-008
Date: 2026-02-01
========================================================================
Follows standard first-aid practice for snakebite in southern Africa.

DO
1. Move away from the snake. Keep the person calm and still.
2. Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the bite (the limb may swell).
3. Keep the bitten limb still, for example with a splint, at about heart level.
4. Get the person to a hospital quickly - antivenom is only given in hospital.
5. If safe, take a photo of the snake. Do not try to catch or kill it.
6. Note the time of the bite and any changes (swelling, drooping eyelids,
   difficulty swallowing or breathing).

DO NOT
- Cut the wound, suck out venom, or apply ice or electric shocks
- Apply a tight tourniquet
- Give alcohol or traditional remedies

SPITTING COBRA - VENOM IN THE EYES
Rinse the eyes with plenty of water (or milk if no water) for 15 minutes and go to
the clinic. Do not rub the eyes.

DANGER SIGNS ON THE WAY TO HOSPITAL
Drooping eyelids, slurred speech, difficulty breathing or swallowing, bleeding from
the gums, or fast spreading swelling. If breathing stops, start rescue breaths/CPR.

Most snakebites happen at night and in long grass. Wear closed shoes and use a torch
when walking outside after dark.
